sources.citation: McHenry, Marisa (ed.). 2013 [printed 2011]. Organised Phonology Data: Topura [Wedau, wed], Milne Bay Province. SIL-PNG, 6 pp. (SIL archive 54003)
sources.note: The section 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)' (p. 4) is empty; no stress marks in the sample text. Topura dialect.

sources.citation: Ezard, Bryan. 1997. A grammar of Tawala, an Austronesian language of the Milne Bay area, Papua New Guinea. Pacific Linguistics C-137. (ANU hdl 1885/145950)
sources.note: Sec. 4.5 p. 44: 'Stress in Tawala is predictable, occurring on the penultimate (second to last) syllable' -- this is TAWALA [tbo, tawa1288], not Wedau. Its 15 Wedau mentions are lexical/comparative (Ezard read King 1901); none concern stress.

sources.citation: Lithgow, David. 1976. Austronesian languages: Milne Bay and adjacent islands (Milne Bay Province). In Wurm (ed.), NGALLS vol. 2, 441-523. Pacific Linguistics C-39.
sources.note: Para 84 STRESS (p. 475), Papuan Tip Cluster-wide only: 'In all of the languages of PTC it seems that stress is predictable within certain word-classes, notably kinship nouns and verbs. When a kinship noun is pluralised by the addition of a suffix, the stress moves one syllable closer to the end of the word...'. No Wedau-specific default position.

sources.citation: Church of England in Australia. 1935. First reader in Wedau. (ANU Open Research digitised copy, hdl 1885/207702)
sources.note: Primer lessons only; no pronunciation preface, no stress marks.

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Wedau language' (en), accessed 2026-09-17
sources.note: No phonology; cites only Ethnologue, Kahn 1993 and King 1901.

sources.citation: Easton, Catherine. 2007. Discourses of orthography development: community-based practice in Milne Bay (P.N.G.). PhD thesis, La Trobe University. doi:10.26181/5fb5bf5e92b5f
sources.note: Ch. 5 phonology of the Wedau-to-Galuwahi chain; sec. 5.3 (printed p. 121-122): 'I do not discuss stress for two reasons. Firstly, it requires a more focussed study in order to analyse the stress and intonation patterns that differ between villages...'. Sec. 8.2 (pp. 208-209): speakers say Taupota differs from Wedau in 'tune' (stress + intonation). Explicitly silent on placement.

sources.citation: Ross, Malcolm. 1988. Proto Oceanic and the Austronesian languages of western Melanesia. Pacific Linguistics C-98.
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: open copy online: WID Offsite Storage PL6201.R67 1988 (also: archive.org controlled lending)
sources.note: Wedau appears only in sound-correspondence tables and reconstructions; no stress statement.

sources.citation: Clarke, Emily. 1977. Missionary lingue franche: Wedau. In S. A. Wurm (ed.), New Guinea area languages and language study, vol. 3, 953-970. Pacific Linguistics C-40. DOI 10.15144/PL-C40.953
sources.note: Sec. 7.4.5.11.2.1 Phonology (pp. 954-955) lists vowels 'long or short', consonants, CV/CVm syllables; no mention of stress, accent, pitch or intonation (verified with whitespace-stripped search). Bibliography names Capell n.d. 'An Introduction to the Wedau Language' (typed notes).

sources.citation: Capell, Arthur. 1976. Austronesian and Papuan 'mixed' languages: general remarks. In Wurm (ed.), NGALLS vol. 2, 527-579. Pacific Linguistics C-39.
sources.note: Wedau forms in comparative tables only; silent on stress.

sources.citation: Fox, C. E. 1910. An introduction to the study of the Oceanic languages. London: SPCK. (archive.org introductiontost00foxcuoft)
sources.note: Wedau cited for the article -na and the interdental l; nothing on accent.

sources.citation: Ray, Sidney H. 1907. The Melanesian languages of British New Guinea. In Reports of the Cambridge Anthropological Expedition to Torres Straits, vol. III: Linguistics, 413-503. Cambridge: CUP.
sources.note: Phonology notes pp. 417-419 cite King's Wedau Grammar p. 5 for consonants (g', interdental l, t/d before i); no accent or stress statement for Wedau anywhere in the scanned text.
